claims.text: A machine-learning-driven high-throughput design pipeline can identify novel low-density refractory high-entropy alloys with simultaneously high strength and good ductility.
Combining computational prediction of microstructure stability with experimental validation enables the identification of such alloys.
A database-trained combinatorial machine-learning model integrated with CALPHAD or first-principles data can propose compositions that optimize strength, ductility, and density.
Comparable synthesis, homogenization, and heat-treatment conditions can produce stable microstructures suitable for mechanical testing.
Selecting appropriate principal refractory elements and fine-tuning their fractions facilitates stable single- or dual-phase solid-solution microstructures.
The model can infer composition–structure–property relationships from existing data.
The inferred relationships enable the model to optimize the balance of lattice distortion, configurational entropy, and solid-solution strengthening.
Machine-learning prediction reduces trial-and-error synthesis when seeking favorable mechanical performance.
The designed alloys will exhibit a yield-strength increase greater than 10% over compositions obtained by conventional trial-and-error methods.
The designed alloys will retain notable ductility.
The designed alloys will have densities a few percent lower than comparable commercial refractory alloys.
Traditional trial-and-error or purely computational approaches make slower progress in discovering RHEAs that combine mechanical performance with reduced weight.
The pipeline requires representative training data.
Prediction accuracy may decline for compositions and microstructures far outside the training distribution.
Prediction accuracy may decline when thermodynamic models are poorly parameterized for novel chemistries.
Limited training data and variations in processing conditions prevent exact determination of the expected mechanical-property improvements.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome requires a yield-strength improvement greater than 10% and a density reduction, whereas the falsification rule allows merely matching the baseline. Matching the baseline would fail to demonstrate the stated improvements but would not refute the hypothesis under the proposed rule.
